occupants.note: SEATED BY THE PLACEMENT POLICY'S PLATTED DEAL (data/reconstruction/1835_platted_seats.json, dealt by T-1613 and carried onto this roof by T-1685; liberties L270 and L276). NO SOURCE PLACES THIS HOUSEHOLD HERE, OR ANYWHERE. Its own record gives a name and no address — no street, no lot and not even a division — so both halves of its band were dealt rather than read, and the lot under this roof is the policy's labourer_dwellings clause answered on the committed plat: blk_randolph_franklin#03, fronting washington, a standing roof of family D1 the clause admits. THE SOURCES BELOW CARRY THE NAME AND NOTHING ELSE. The roof's own existence, position and footprint remain conjectural and are unchanged by the seating — it is still a count-unit of the 665-roof programme, adopted rather than raised, so nothing was drawn off the reconstruction order book. The household's id is carried in resident_assignment rather than in this prose, because tools/generate_dooryard_pickets.py admits a lot for a garden on an id appearing HERE and a keeper a policy deal seats is not a measurement of anybody's garden.

persons.name: J. A. Marshall
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'A. MARSHALL' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 19 November 1834, column 4. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `schoolteacher` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Marshall, James A. | 1832, | London, Eng. | 70 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS2A — one bearer of the surname, the forename initial agrees, and the resident's own record spells the roster's forename 'james' — the discriminator the roster's initials do not supply (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Marshall, James A., 2906 Indiana avenue, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS2A — one bearer of the surname, the forename initial agrees, and the resident's own record spells the roster's forename 'james' — the discriminator the roster's initials do not supply (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Marshall, Mrs. J. A. | Letter. | June 30, 1848. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0701, printed page 193), admitted 1848-06-30 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Marshall' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins J. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name J. A. Marshall as a schoolteacher at Chicago 1 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

citations.citation: Early Chicago: Reception to the Settlers of Chicago Prior to 1840, by the Calumet Club, of Chicago, Tuesday Evening, May 27, 1879 (Chicago: Calumet Club, 1879) — the printed proceedings of the FIRST old-settlers' reception, with the registry of settlers who signed it.
what_it_supplies: the date, host and criterion of the first reception, 27 May 1879
the club's own count of 149 settlers who registered during the evening

the printed REGISTER itself, pages 84-90: 159 entries, each with the man's name, his own date of arrival in Chicago, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address — the only roster in the series that dates its people
the three aggregate tables of printed page 72 — places of birth, years of arrival and ages — each summing to 149, read off the plate rather than the OCR
what_it_does_not_supply: a residence in 1835. A date of arrival here is what the man said in 1879, forty to sixty years after the fact, and the club's criterion reaches to the end of 1839

which of the 159 printed entries are the 'few [who] called afterward and signed the registry' and are therefore outside the 149 the tables count — the plate does not mark them, and this project does not guess
an address in 1835: the register's fifth column is the 1879 post-office address

citations.citation: The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1 (November 26, 1833) through Vol. II, No. 18 (August 26, 1835). Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, editor and publisher. Seventy-three issues, OCR-assisted research transcriptions from page scans.
what_it_supplies: that a named trade was being carried on in Chicago in a named week, and often where
self-reported addresses, which are the strongest address evidence this project has: the advertiser was paying, and his customers had to find him
dissolution, removal and replacement notices — the only thing that keeps a documented business out of the 1835 town under the owner's ruling 3
post-office letter lists, naming residents by the hundred (ruling 1: a listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged letter_list_only)
the village and later town ordinances, printed complete — the 7 November 1833 code is the richest single item in the run
arrivals and clearances, which date the piers and the harbour as working structures
public notices that fix a building as a polling place, an auction site or a meeting place on a given day
the paper's own imprint, self-reported: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
twenty-one months of continuous weekly attestation ending three weeks before the scene date, including the issue printed on 1835-07-01
what_it_does_not_supply: any building's form, material, storey count, fenestration or dimensions — an advertisement describes a trade, not a building
the specific corner of any junction it names: 'on the corner of' does not say which of the four
anything at all from an engraving — see trap 1; the cuts are the printer's stock
proof that a business named in 1833 or 1834 still stood on 1835-07-01; that is ruling 3's survival liberty, and it is a liberty
an argument from silence, unless corpus.json shows the issues either side of the silence are both in the deposit
a reading that outranks a scan read of the same passage — see ruling 2 and the C. & I. HARMON case
a citation without an issue page and column

citations.citation: Chicago Tribune, May 19, 1882, report of the Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to “The Old Settlers of Chicago”, held 18 May 1882, with the list “Names of Old Settlers Present, Residents and of Age Prior to 1840” and the speeches of Vice-President J. W. Doane and the Hon. John Wentworth.
what_it_supplies: 128 named men who were of age and living in Chicago before 1 January 1840, and where each of them lived in 1882
the club's own arithmetic of the settler population: 414 known old settlers, 35 dead in the year, 118 in the house, 160 at the third reception
a handful of trades and firsts attached to the year's dead — a Fort Dearborn gunsmith, the first grist-mill, the first mail rider to Milwaukee, the first frame building west of the river
what_it_does_not_supply: a year of arrival for any guest
an 1835 address: every address printed is of 1882

Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.
A required distinction between named documentary landmarks and anonymous inferred infill.
what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

citations.citation: The Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, June 1st, 1842, to June 1st, 1892 (Chicago: Knight, Leonard & Co., 1892), John C. Grant, editor — the semi-centennial volume of the congregation, read from the Princeton Theological Seminary copy digitised by the Internet Archive as item secondpresbyterian00chic
what_it_supplies: 2,255 lines of a Chicago church roll running from 1 June 1842 to 1892 — a name, how the member was admitted (profession or letter), the date, and for the closed roll a remark (dismissed, deceased, ordained).
962 distinct surnames, of which 938 lines carry a surname this project already holds from the town of 1835.
The founding cohort of 1 June 1842, which is where the overlap with the 1835 town is thickest: W. H. Brown, George W. Dole and Mrs A. N. Fullerton are all on the first day's roll.
A dated Chicago appearance for a surname, which is exactly the kind of second source the resident sweep files as a lead.
what_it_does_not_supply: An 1835 residency, or any part of one. The earliest line on the roll is seven years after the scene date and the ratified ladder never makes an 1835 resident from a later appearance alone.

A woman's own name, much of the time. The roll sets a wife as `Mrs.` followed by her HUSBAND'S name — `Fullerton, Mrs. A. N.` — so a line that meets a man in the 1835 layer has met his name and not him, and the crosswalk flags every such line.
A death or a departure that can be dated. `Deceased` and `Dismissed` are the state of the roll at its closing on 1 June 1892, not events with dates of their own.
An address, a trade or a household. The roll carries none of the three.
